heading: Some interpretable features and circuits recur across models
definition: the same interpretable features or circuits (neurons, SAE features) recur across different models.
summary: Several independent groups find recurring subsets of interpretable features and circuits across models. Broader recurrence is contested: some comparisons fail to match neurons or find shared circuit mechanisms across model families.

suggested_status.by_scale: Toy: R2 for recurring abstract feature forms, with specific identities limited. <1B: R2 for selected SAE features; C for the tested Pythia–Mamba neuron/activation basis. 1-10B: R2 for selective feature recurrence; C for unrestricted circuit recurrence across families. 10-100B: R0 for the reported relation-defined head operations, including Llama-3.1-70B. >100B: ?; no stated coverage.
suggested_status.reason: Selective recurrence has support from Pythia–Mamba SAE matching (arXiv:2410.06672#R1) and restricted harmonic theory (arXiv:2312.08550#r1). Pythia–Mamba neuron/activation matching instead reports essentially absent similarity, with mean MPPC 0.30 (arXiv:2410.06672#R2): this condition is challenges, rather than limits_scope. The unrestricted circuit reading is also contested by failure of the Qwen numerical-comparison mechanism to recur in Llama/Gemma (10.18653/v1/2026.acl-srw.84#R13; 10.18653/v1/2026.acl-srw.84#R14). The checks reclassify two further conditions from limits_scope to challenges: tense, which the authors interpret as not emerging in English copying auto-encoders (arXiv:1811.01157#r21), and named substrate axes, which fail to recur between vision and language despite aligned coarse geometry (arXiv:2606.07882#r4). by_scale does not place these two, because the pack gives no parameter counts for them. arXiv:2410.06672, arXiv:1811.01157 and arXiv:2606.07882 share no authors with an original. Thus C records concrete challenges alongside R2 evidence for recurring subsets. Counts: versions.V5.verdicts.challenges.studies=1 reflects the index verdicts, in which only 10.18653/v1/2026.acl-srw.84 has a V5 challenges verdict. It precedes the checker's reclassifications of arXiv:2410.06672#R2, arXiv:1811.01157#r21 and arXiv:2606.07882#r4, so it is not a corrected total, and no corrected total is computed here. All counts quoted here were built before the checker's corrections. versions.V5.studies_by_size has <1B, 1-10B and 10-100B coverage but no >100B; versions.V5.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original=1, so author-overlap extensions should not count as independent. Larger-model head-role evidence (arXiv:2412.11965#R4; arXiv:2412.11965#R8) directly tests V5 using vocabulary-projected parameters, relation scores and head counts: T2, different method and same question, rather than T3. This tranche correction alone does not establish independent replication at 10-100B.
suggested_status.open_questions: Would matched, independently pretrained models with controlled task competence reproduce the same causally validated circuit across families? Would independently fitted dictionaries preserve feature semantics and intervention effects after accounting for thresholds, layer selection and matching nulls? Tests above 100B and at reasoning/preference-training stages would change the scale-specific assessment.

source.title: Convergent Learning: Do different neural networks learn the same representations?
source.authors: Yi-Xuan Li; J. Yosinski; J. Clune; Hod Lipson; J. Hopcroft

original_result.setup: The study grouped units from the two networks, Net1 and Net2, by correlations across networks and visually inspected selected groups.
original_result.result: Selected clusters shared Gabor filters, edge orientations, and color blobs. One conv2 cluster contained three Net1 units and three Net2 units with similar features involving red and magenta objects.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: DQN and Rainbow learned visually similar edge detectors and Pong features.
Parentheses and tense neurons recurred across translation models.
ICA recovered shared semantic axes across languages and embedding models.
Symmetry-based Fourier-like features (group harmonics) provably recurred in invariant models meeting the theorem's conditions.
Attention heads predicting the next item in ordered sequences recurred across model families.
Neuron tuning aligned above chance across vision architectures and training datasets.
Attention heads implementing strongly encoded relations recurred across language model families.
Separately fitted genealogical subspaces had causal effects across five Llama and Gemma models.
Canonical spatial eigenvectors recurred across tested VGG training settings.
Compatible syllogistic reasoning mechanisms recurred across GPT-2, Pythia and Llama models.
Matched SAE features aligned above random baselines in Pythia and Gemma middle layers.
A variable-assignment feature persisted across base, fine-tuned and merged models.
Interpretable neuron families recurred across GPT2 and Pythia training seeds.
Pythia and Mamba shared strongly matched SAE features at proportional depths.
Interpretable feature groups recurred across multimodal encoders and partly across text encoders.
Pizza and Clock representations closely matched, with disc or circle topology recurring across seeds.
Most visual concepts in the next-to-last layer were substantially similar across tested model pairs.
Gemma models shared aligned features in middle layers and compatible semantic subspaces.
Sparse visual components shared category motifs across architectures and training objectives.
Sinusoidal first-layer neurons recurred across MLPs and the tested transformer variants.
Selected entropy-related and attention-disabling features kept their functions when transferred between GPT2 models.
Over 1,000 shared concepts activated across three vision models trained with different objectives.
Nearly all Mamba SAE features had Pythia matches above the study's threshold.
Recurring visual dimensions were interpretable and organized by object categories.
Matched SAE features validated most strongly in structured domains and larger models.
Emergent misalignment fine-tunes shared several highly ranked attention heads.
Matched health-related components showed consistent patterns across model pairs.
Qwen models used attention heads to introduce a separable greater-than signal.
Thousands of selective neurons recurred across independently trained language and vision model families.
Intermediate SAE decoder features showed extensive cross-model cosine matching.
Matched sparse features correlated far above permutation baselines across model pairs.
A shared SAE dictionary produced aligned latents and consistent labels across language model families.
Most listed features of EEG signals were encoded and causally used across three architectures.
A causally validated grammatical number axis recurred across six language models.
Code models shared concept-circuit rankings and information-flow types.
SAE decoder features showed strong cosine matches across training seeds.
Feature recurrence weakened across training algorithms and deeper Atari network layers.
Parentheses and tense neuron recurrence depended on translation language and training objective.
Shared representation families contained different specific features across MLPs, Transformers and seeds.
Successor mechanisms were absent in GPT-2 Large and failed on some held-out sequences.
VAE methods differed in how they encoded horizontal viewing angles and allocated latent channels.
Relational attention heads recurred unevenly and were scarce for weakly encoded operations.
Syllogistic circuits changed location in Qwen and recurred incompletely in low-capability models.
SAE alignment weakened under representational similarity analysis and varied across semantic subspaces and layers.
Few base features persisted through fine-tuning and merging, even among closely related models.
Only a small minority of neurons recurred across training seeds.
Feature matching weakened for RWKV, complex features and raw neuron activations.
Shared multimodal features overlapped little with differently trained vision encoders.
Modular-addition models differed significantly in phase distributions despite shared coarse topology.
Important visual concepts remained model-specific, and sharing declined with depth and training differences.
Gemma alignment weakened outside middle layers and failed for an incompatible semantic subspace.
Modular-addition models shared a general structure but differed in deeper features and circuits.
Some semantic SAE features failed to transfer or reversed across language models.
Many vision concepts remained model-specific despite an objective encouraging shared representations.
Matched Mamba and Pythia features fired on fewer than half the same inputs.
Even the most recurring visual dimension fell well below the maximum similarity achievable within models.
Only about half of safety SAE features recurred across six models.
Feature validation weakened for the smaller model and general-text domains.
Emergent misalignment fine-tunes shared only part of their highest-ranked attention circuitry.
Health-related components were less similar when models differed in both input type and architecture.
Finer numerical-comparison circuitry varied within Qwen and reproduced weakly in some models.
Recurring neurons formed a shrinking minority of model neurons.
Feature matching weakened near Pythia's output, and firing correspondence remained limited after rotation.
Independent SAE matching and transferred labels showed weaker correspondence than shared-dictionary latents.
Named semantic axes did not recur between vision and language models.
Some features of EEG signals varied by task and model, peaking in different layers.
Shared code concepts occupied different layer bands and developed differently across models.
SAE encoders failed to transfer directly between seeds without rotating activations.
Qwen's numerical-comparison circuit did not generalize to Llama and Gemma.

counting_note: Each group counts distinct sources for this claim. The same source can appear in more than one group or claim; counts are not votes.

untested.what: Recurrence of interpretable features or circuits above 100B parameters.
untested.basis: counts: versions.V5.studies_by_size and versions.V5.coverage_by_operation.*.by_size contain no >100B entry. This identifies a gap in recorded size coverage; studies with size not stated remain unclassified.

untested.what: Feature or circuit recurrence specifically tested across reasoning-stage or preference/RL-stage language models.
untested.basis: counts: versions.V5.studies_by_stage and versions.V5.coverage_by_operation.*.by_stage contain neither reasoning nor preference/RL. Atari agents supply reinforcement-learning evidence, but do not cover these language-model training stages.

untested.what: Verification of shared interpretable semantics for statistically corresponding units, SAE features and spatial covariance eigenvector patterns in these measurements.
untested.basis: arXiv:2311.09466#R3 and arXiv:2311.09466#R4 report above-chance unit-tuning alignment between ResNet20 and VGG16, with the comparison's training dataset unspecified. arXiv:2605.28870#r1 reports matched SAE-feature correlations above an object-permutation null. arXiv:2409.19460#R9 reports recurring VGG spatial covariance eigenvector patterns. None verifies recurrence of shared interpretable features or circuits; the checks assign cannot_determine and no V5 link.

wording_issues.issue: SAE-space work explicitly targets weak/analogous universality, and genealogy probes are fitted separately per model. These findings do not establish feature identity.

A recurring algorithmic template or head role need not imply recurring concrete circuitry. Modular-addition architectures differ below the abstract template; numerical comparison fails to preserve the Qwen mechanism across families.

The evidence mixes independent pretraining, seed replicas, shared-base fine-tunes and jointly trained dictionaries. These conditions provide different tests of spontaneous recurrence. The jointly trained dictionary contains shared and model-preferring concepts, establishing partial recurrence across the full dictionary rather than complete universality.

These are not interchangeable units of evidence. Pythia–Mamba matching is strong after SAE decomposition but judged absent in the neuron/activation basis. High SAE decoder cosine can also coexist with weak firing correspondence.

Universal can mean a recurring subset, recurrence within a selected model group, or graded best-match similarity. The neuron results concern a minority, while visual-dimension recurrence remains below its within-model ceiling.

method_sensitivity.what: Pythia–Mamba SAE matching averages MPPC 0.74 versus 0.30 for neuron/activation matching. The authors describe similarity in the neuron/activation basis as essentially absent, a challenges condition for V5. ICA axes align more clearly than PCA axes in fastText/BERT and vision comparisons.

The same paired features can score much higher under SVCCA than RSA. For Pythia Time, the scores are 0.59 and 0.10. Gemma middle-layer RSA is 0.15–0.20 despite SVCCA 0.64–0.71. The Gemma results indicate partial recurrence under V5, observed metric dependence under V6 and observed incomplete alignment under V7.

Gemma SAE correspondence is strongest in middle layers. Early-layer SVCCA is 0.35 ± 0.05; average SVCCA at Gemma-2-9B L39 is 0.374. These are partial recurrence under V5 and observed incomplete alignment under V7. Visual concept correspondence often declines with depth. Pythia decoder-feature matching also falls at the site before unembedding.

Validated SAE correspondence varies sharply between structured and general-text domains. Of 240 preselected question_answering pairs, 7.9% pass validation, indicating partial correspondence. Cohen's d −0.011 measures domain discriminability; no domain-specific null establishes absent correspondence. Simple token features have stronger activation matching than complex features, although complex features can retain matching semantic themes. Stitched structural features transfer more consistently than semantic features.

Reversing Pythia–Mamba matching changes mean MPPC from 0.74 to 0.78; strong recurrence persists, giving observed V5 recurrence and partial V6 direction dependence. More permissive mutual top-k neuron matching increases matched counts while scaling persists. Pythia–OPT exponents are 0.68 at k=1, 0.75 at k=2, 0.78 at k=5 and 0.71 at k=10. Diffusion–OpenCLIP exponents are 0.63 at k=1 and 0.61 at k=2. These settings change counts without showing weakening or disappearance of the scaling trend.

USAE and SharedSAE encourage cross-model sharedness during optimization. USAE's normalized-entropy distribution peaks at 1 and 0.6, with over 1000 concepts at peak entropy; shared and model-preferring concepts indicate partial V5 universality and observed V7 partial convergence. SharedSAE's solo-selection agreement remains affected by training losses. Its pairwise solo-TopK median is 31.5 of 50 on 300k positions, requiring at least 50 selections in both pair members; the all-four median is 26 of 50 on a 100k-position window. Dedicated per-model dictionaries provide a weaker correspondence comparator.

method_sensitivity.factor: Rotation and the measured feature property
method_sensitivity.what: In arXiv:2605.24577, decoder-column matching and post-rotation feature firing give different assessments of recurrence. Pythia decoder matching is high at intermediate sites and falls at the final site; feature firing remains only partially aligned after rotation. Decoder geometry alone does not establish semantic identity or shared causal roles.

Universal-neuron prevalence uses an acknowledged unprincipled cutoff. Mamba/Pythia binary-Jaccard alignment uses a post-hoc cutoff without a null. Steering-transfer validation rates are conditional on prior MNN pair selection rather than all extracted features.

Changing vision training data or pretraining qualifies concept sharing. Adding Stanford Cars increases concept dissimilarity in both directions. ImageNet pretraining followed by NABirds fine-tuning produces the most dissimilar concepts among the ResNet-18 training comparisons: partial V5 sharing and observed V7 training dependence. Tense-neuron correspondence is weaker for Chinese-target translation; the authors interpret tense as not emerging in English copying auto-encoders, an absent V5 result and challenges condition, with signed correlations −0.33, −0.19 and −0.03. EEG feature recurrence depends on task.

SharedSAE activation agreement exceeds its functional-score agreement and promoted-token overlap. Stitched attention-deactivation features retain an inspected role while their effective-null-space norm fraction changes from 0.27 to 0.77.

status_amendment.public_note: The rationale now also names two results that the checks reclassified as challenges to universal features: the authors' reading that tense information does not emerge in English auto-encoders trained only to copy their input, and named axes that fail to match between vision and language models; it also says the automatic tallies predate these corrections. The level stays at C.
